newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Macau gang warfare seen not spilling into Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Macau gang warfare seen not spilling into Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong police said on Monday they were keeping an eye on a wave of bombings, arson and drive-by shootings sweeping nearby Macau, but the crime spree was not showing signs of spilling over into the British colony.
"Hong Kong crime has fallen to a 15 year low," a Hong Kong police spokesman said.

Police declined to officially comment on liaison with overseas jurisdictions, but officers said privately that a close eye was trained on nearby Macau and intelligence about known criminals was being passed on.
Hong Kong people fret about the prospect of corruption and cronyism, endemic in China's business world, spreading across the border after Hong Kong is handed back to Beijing at midnight on June 30.
But fears of a get-rich-quick crime wave sweeping the territory ahead of the handover have failed to materialise.
Police Commissioner Eddie Hui said the number of offences, particularly violent crimes, had fallen 14 percent in 1996 making Hong Kong one of the world's safest cities.

Instead it is Macau, where Sino-Portuguese relations over the transition have been amiable in contrast to hostility between Britain and China over Hong Kong, which is being rocked by gang-related warfare.

Signs of trouble in Macau emerged in late 1994 when a Hong Kong gangster, Anderly Chan, known as "the Tiger of Wanchai" was gunned down in the enclave. It simmered through 1995 and began to boil over about six months ago.

Violence peaked again over the weekend. Three men -- police suspect them to be members of one of the larger triads, or Chinese criminal secret societies -- were gunned down in broad daylight by assailants mounted on motorcycles.
Macau, a tiny 21 sq km (eight sq mile) territory of just 450,000 people, experienced a 19.4 percent rise in crime last year. Crime rose 20 percent in 1995, government figures show.
Both Hong Kong and Macau are foreign-run enclaves perched on the south coast of China in the throes of transition.
The British hand Hong Kong to China in just 57 days time.
Macau, a Portuguese toehold in Asia for more than 400 years, reverts to China in December 1999.
But there their similarities end. Hong Kong's 6.4 million people reside in one of the world's great economic powerhouses.
The stock market ranks seventh world wide in capitalisation and is the second largest in Asia.
Its foreign exchange market is the world's fifth largest in terms of daily turnover and its banking system is the fifth largest when it comes to external transactions.

These activities have made Hong Kong rich. Per capita gross domestic product at close to $25,000 compares with Macau's nominal US$16,000 -- much of it derived from casino taxes which form the mainstay of the economy.
Taxes on casino takings account for nearly half of Macau's gross domestic product and offer tempting pickings for organised crime, government figures show.

Police in Macau blame the outbreak of violence, which began to gather pace in 1994, on two main triad societies -- the 14K and Sai Fong -- fighting a turf war over casino-related loansharking, smuggling, protection rackets and prostitution.
Competition has intensified as Macau's economy, particularly its property sector suffered a downturn. Property analysts say there are 30,000 apartments lying idle in Macau.
Competition is intensifying further as criminals from fast developing southern China trickle across Macau's porous border to seek part of the action, police said.
